description: We are Delta Detectives from Bangladesh, working on "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" Our project, "My Climate Story," uses NASA satellite imagery and climate data to help students see how their own area has changed, in simple Bangla and English. We are looking for university students who want to join us.
summary:
My Climate Story is a Bangla-and-English web app that helps school students in Bangladesh see how their own place has changed, using NASA data. A student picks one of 12 locations on a map, slides between Landsat satellite images from 1990 and 2025, and reads local temperature trends for 2001-2025 from NASA POWER next to NASA GISTEMP's global temperature record. Short quizzes and a ready-made classroom guide turn the data into a lesson for teachers.

For the Earth System Trend Detective challenge, we used NASA data to find and explain trends at a local level. We cleaned and checked the data first, found its limits (a data shift around 1997-2000, a short 25-year record, and a rainfall jump around 2015-16), and built those limits into the app. It tells students plainly when a trend is not statistically significant.

It matters because the young people who will live with climate change the longest rarely see it explained in their own language, for their own place. Because it relies only on open NASA datasets, it can work for any location on Earth.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Climate change is usually taught as a global story: average temperatures, melting glaciers, rising seas. Students in Bangladesh notice something closer to home, like rivers that shift, summers that feel hotter and monsoons that arrive differently. Most climate material is in English, packed with charts and built for fast internet, so the young people who will live with climate change the longest have the fewest ways to understand what is changing around them.

WHAT WE BUILT

My Climate Story tells a local, personal climate story in Bangla and English. A student chooses a place from our map of 12 locations across Bangladesh, and the app walks them through it step by step:

1. Then and now: a before-and-after slider compares Landsat satellite images (30 m) of the same place from January 1990 and February 2025, so students can spot changes in rivers, buildings and vegetation.

2. Temperature: a chart of the local record for 2001-2025, shown by year or by month, with a plain-language reading of whether the trend is statistically significant.

3. Rain: seasonal rainfall for the same place.

4. Our shared planet: NASA GISTEMP's global temperature record, so students can connect their local story to the global one.

5. Learn by playing: short quizzes where every answer comes with an explanation.

6. For teachers: a classroom guide of about 35 minutes, with learning goals and discussion prompts.

Students can also save the stories they like. The site is hosted on Vercel.

HOW WE USED NASA DATA

Landsat scenes power the before-and-after slider. Monthly NASA POWER data gives local temperature and rainfall for each location, which we downloaded through the POWER API, then cleaned and checked before building anything. For example, Dhaka's monthly data can be reproduced from this API call: https://power.larc.nasa.gov/api/temporal/monthly/point?parameters=T2M,T2M_MAX,T2M_MIN,PRECTOTCORR,RH2M&community=AG&longitude=90.4125&latitude=23.8103&start=1981&end=2025&format=JSON

NASA GISTEMP v4 gives the global context. Full links are in the Data used and References sections.

WHAT THE DATA TAUGHT US

Checking the data changed how we designed the app, and we show these limits to students instead of hiding them:

- Most cities show a jump in temperature around 1997-2000 that looks like a change in the data, not in the climate. We only calculate trends from 2001.

- Twenty-five years is short. Most local temperature trends are not statistically significant, and the app says so plainly. Cox's Bazar is the clear exception, at about +0.17 degrees C per decade.

- POWER rainfall jumps around 2015-16 in almost every city, so we do not draw rainfall trends from it.

- GISTEMP is a global record. We use it as context and never as a stand-in for local temperature.

We would rather show students an honest "not sure yet" than a confident chart that turns out to be wrong. Learning to read uncertain data is part of what we want them to take away.

CHALLENGE IT ANSWERS

Earth System Trend Detective: we use NASA Earth observation and climate data to find and explain trends at a local level, and we are open about where the data is weak.

WHO IT HELPS

Our main users are students (roughly grades 6 to 10) and their teachers. Because the app relies only on global, open NASA datasets, it can work anywhere on Earth, from the Mekong Delta to the Nile Delta to the Pacific Islands. Adding a new language needs only translated text, and teachers need no special equipment to use it in class.

WHAT WE WOULD BUILD NEXT

- Rainfall trends using NASA GPM IMERG data.

- A teacher dashboard and more lesson plans.

- Community photos to compare with satellite views.

- Future projections using NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6.

- Offline mode and SMS or WhatsApp summaries for very low-connectivity areas.
